# Receipt Wrecker

> A single-file web tool that turns words or a picture into a Twitch chat message that
> prints big on a streamer's thermal receipt printer, when that printer is driven by
> SassyTP's printer-bot (a Streamer.bot action). The user pastes the message into chat as a
> cheer.

AI crawlers and LLM agents are welcome to read, index, and cite this site. The tool is open
source under the MIT license and everything below is public.

Key facts:

- Live site: https://receipt.uwutoowo.com
- Source: https://github.com/shamu4life/receipt-wrecker
- License: MIT
- Current version: 1.6.0 (2026-10-14). Before 1.0.0 the tool targeted a different printer
  bot (nutty.gg's); that support was removed.
- No accounts, no analytics, no third-party services.
- Each message is at most 500 characters, Twitch's limit. Longer work is split across
  several cheers rather than truncated.

## How the printer bot treats a cheer

SassyTP's printer-bot draws each cheer on a receipt page in Edge, screenshots it at the
printer's dot width (576 dots on 80 mm paper, 384 on 58 mm), dithers it to black and white
and prints it.

- A cheer of at least the streamer's High Roller threshold (default 25 bits; 0 turns it off)
  is a High Roller cheer: the message is read as HTML and passed through an allow-list
  sanitizer, so inline styles print.
- A smaller cheer prints as plain 16px text inside quote marks (since Printer Bot 3.0.0 its tags
  are left out and its words printed; before, the markup was printed too).
- Printer Bot 3.0 adds a per-printer switch, "Allow High Roller prints", on by
  default. A printer with it off prints every cheer as plain text, so the tool has the same
  switch among the streamer's settings and builds every block in its plain form when it is off.
- Printer Bot 3.0 can also print on Letter paper through an ordinary printer, and its rules can
  send big cheers there. Since 1.6.0 the tool models one such Letter printer: cheers of the bits
  its rule starts at are built for its page (7.5 inches wide, 400 CSS px at 53.3 px to the inch,
  one page a cheer) in its layout, "Scaled like 80 mm" (about 6 cm for the message under the
  profile picture) or "Large message" (about 16 cm, laid out from the left, so blocks centre
  themselves), and every smaller cheer on the roll. Its Allow High Roller prints is taken as on.

The streamer's settings (paper width, threshold, bits per inch, maximum length, Printer
Bot 3.0's Allow High Roller prints, and since 1.6.0 a Letter printer's bits, layout, image fit
and print profile) are not visible from chat, so the tool asks the user to enter them, with SassyTP's defaults filled
in. Changing a Big text or Sideways text setting, or Glyph-art's Characters, Detail or Smooth
shading, while the bits are below the threshold raises the bits to the threshold (or offers to,
for a big jump), and the block says so, with an Undo after a raise. It never raises when the
streamer's roll printer has Allow High Roller prints off, since no amount helps, unless the
threshold's cheer reaches the Letter printer, which the block then says.

## What it outputs

- Big text (High Roller): the words in the font the block picks (since 1.4.0: Arial Bold, the
  default, Arial Black, Impact, Comic Sans MS, Georgia, Times New Roman, Courier New, Trebuchet
  MS, Verdana or Tahoma, all on every Windows PC and each measured), as large as the paper's width allows
  (leaving room for a j's hook or an f's arm at a line's ends), as
  typed, with the words wrapped to the paper, stacked one letter per line, or each line at its
  own size; optionally upside down.
  Example: `Cheer100 <div style="\66ont:700 70px/.8 Arial">HELLO</div>` (the CSS property name "font" is written \66ont to pass this channel's chat filter; see below).
- Sideways text (High Roller): the words running down the tape using CSS writing-mode; each
  typed line becomes a column, centred across the paper by its ink, worked out from the font's
  own measurements (most blocks get a small `position:relative;left` shift; a column whose bottom end is a
  letter that draws past its own space, such as an f's arm or a j's hook, gets a
  `padding-bottom` so the bot's box doesn't cut it). Top to bottom (read by turning the receipt
  anticlockwise) or bottom to top (turn it clockwise; needs Edge 132 or newer on the
  streamer's PC).
- Glyph-art (High Roller): a picture as a grid of characters: Han characters in a square
  grid, ASCII letters or block characters in Courier New rows, or Braille.
- Han text as typed (plain text, any cheer): the Han characters the user types or pastes,
  printed as themselves in rows of exactly 15 (9 on 58 mm), at any cheer size, up to about 480 a
  cheer with the streamer's length settings at 0. Only Han characters go in, the only ones a full cell
  wide in every CJK font: kana, Hangul, CJK punctuation, Latin letters and the rest are left out
  and named, since they would push the rows out of line.
- Big text's wrap layout breaks a run of Han, kana or Hangul between its characters, never
  before a closing mark or after an opening one; Latin words never break, full-width ones
  included.
- Han tiling (plain): words or a picture drawn out of Han characters as plain text, exactly
  15 characters per line on 80 mm paper (9 on 58 mm), with the cheer word at the end. Below
  the High Roller threshold, Big text and Sideways text print in this form automatically, and a
  glyph-art picture as a plain grid of Han characters.
- Colour (since 1.6.0, a Letter printer in its colour profile only): a text colour and a
  background colour for Big text and Sideways text, and a colour for Glyph-art's characters, as
  `color:` and `background-color:` declarations. On the roll and in black and white no colour
  goes out.
- Two one-cheer tests: a High Roller test (one cheer at the threshold) and a Plain test (one
  bit under it, or 1 bit when High Roller is off or the printer doesn't allow High Roller
  prints), each built for the paper its bits reach.

The tool uses only the tags div and pre, with a style attribute: every line or grid row is
its own div, because the same chat filter held a test message that carried a line-break tag
(br). The CSS property name "font" is written with a unicode escape (\66ont) in the style
attribute, since the filter blocks the literal word "font" too; the browser's CSS parser
resolves it back to "font" with no change to what prints. These are two owner-chosen
exceptions for THIS CHANNEL ONLY, documented in the project's CLAUDE.md. It never sends a
picture tag either: the chat filter of the channel it was built for holds the picture tag.
A picture prints as glyph-art, or (since 1.5.0, on Printer Bot 3.0) as itself from a direct
Imgur, Catbox or ImgBB link sent as text in a High Roller cheer, once the streamer switched
that site on in the bot's dock (Advanced, Images in messages); the tool's settings mirror
that choice under "Pictures from links". Below the High Roller threshold such a picture prints
as a plain grid of Han characters.

If a channel blocks the markup, the tool's fallback is plain Han tiling. If chat holds a
message for its words, that is the moderators saying no to the words: the tool's guidance is
not to rework the message or send the words again in another form, Han tiling included. A
free test (the message sent with Cheer-ready off, so no bits are spent) shows what chat lets
through first. A cheer word standing on its own in the text (such as Cheer50) makes any message
a real cheer that Twitch charges for; the tool counts it in the cost it shows.

## The preview

The preview is drawn by SassyTP's printer-bot renderer (MIT), the bot's own receipt page,
embedded in the tool and run in a sandboxed frame with no network access. Since 1.3.0 it is the
newest Printer Bot release's page (Printer Bot 3.0.1 since 1.4.1, layout 202610140456;
3.0.0-beta.7's and beta.6's pages, layouts 202610122236 and 202610110524, print the tool's
messages the same);
Printer Bot 2.5.4's page (202610090056) prints the tool's messages the same on a receipt printer,
apart from a smaller profile picture. The tool builds for a receipt printer and, since 1.6.0, one
Letter printer (3.0's further printers per cheer are not modelled); a cheer for the Letter printer
is drawn on the bot's Letter page, in the layout picked. A thermal view
shows the receipt at the printer's dot width with the bot's own dither methods; on a Letter page,
at 300 dots to the inch, with only the pictures shaded in black and white, or as drawn in colour. Each part's
preview is drawn when it scrolls near the screen, one at a time, so a long stack stays quick.
The preview names the layout version it draws with (the renderer's own VERSION), so a viewer
can compare it with the Renderer version the streamer's dock shows. The circle where the bot puts
the viewer's profile picture shows a grey stand-in (the preview
never asks Twitch for the real one), and the receipt length shown counts it; a receipt whose
viewer has no picture is about 4.8 cm shorter on 80 mm paper, 4.0 cm on 58 mm.

## Copying and presets

- Copy says "Copied" only when the text reached the clipboard; when the browser refuses, the
  part shows its text, selected, to copy by hand.
- Presets save the block stack in the browser and move between browsers as JSON. Import never
  replaces a saved setup: a taken name gets a number, and a setup already saved exactly as it
  is is left out. Loading a preset asks first when the
  blocks on screen are not saved in any preset.

## Privacy

Text in every mode, and a picture picked from disk for glyph-art, never leave the device. Some picture
operations call this project's own Cloudflare Worker and nothing else:

- Pasting a picture link fetches the picture through an image proxy, because a browser canvas
  cannot read another site's pixels directly.
- On a "Real picture" card, picking a file uploads it to Cloudflare KV behind an unguessable
  link that is deleted after 15 minutes, and rotating or adjusting it re-uploads it. That copy
  is only shown on the card: it never prints as a picture.
- A Real picture's Imgur, Catbox or ImgBB link is read through the proxy for its size, and the
  link itself goes into the cheer, so the streamer's Printer Bot fetches the picture from that
  site.

Settings, the block stack and saved presets are kept in the browser's localStorage.
